items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models

By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: A one-line bookmarklet that sends any video page to a downloader
items.summary: I build PullClip, a free browser-based video downloader, and the feature people ask about most is the smallest one: a bookmarklet. You click it on a video page and the same video opens in the downloader, ready to save. Here is the whole thing, how each part works, and why bookmarklets are still worth knowing in 2026. javascript:(function(){location.href='https://pullclipvid.com/?url='+encodeURIComponent(location.href)})(); That is the entire feature. One line. javascript: tells the browser to run the bookmark as code instead of opening it as a web address. (function(){ ... })() is an IIFE (immediately invoked function expression). It keeps any variables out of the page's global scope, so the bookmarklet never clashes with the site's own scripts. location.href (on the right) reads the address of the page you are on. encodeURIComponent() is the part people skip and then wonder why it breaks. Video links are full of ?, & and =. Without encoding, https://site.com/watch?v=abc&t=30 would split the query string, and the downloader would only receive half the link. location.href = ... (on the left) navigates to the downloader with the encoded link in ?url=, and the page fills the input box

items.title: Verifying signed webhooks in Node.js (and why you must)
items.summary: A webhook endpoint is a public URL that changes your database. Anyone who finds it can curl it. If your handler trusts whatever JSON arrives, then "mark order as paid" or "this email bounced, disable the account" is one forged request away. Most providers sign their webhooks for exactly this reason. But a signature only helps if you check it correctly, and there are a few ways to get that wrong without noticing. Your tests still pass, and the endpoint is still open. This post covers how to verify signed webhooks in Node.js properly: How HMAC signatures work and how to check one Why you need a timing-safe comparison The raw-body trap in Express and Next.js (App Router and Pages Router) Replay protection with timestamps Making the handler idempotent The code doesn't depend on any provider. The scheme it assumes (a hex HMAC-SHA256 over timestamp.rawBody, with the timestamp and signature in headers) is common, and it maps closely onto most providers' formats. Without verification, your endpoint believes three things it has no reason to believe: That the request came from your provider. items.summary: On 3 November I looked at 14 days of visitor data for one form on my site. Five people had started filling it in and never finished. Four of them had pressed Continue with Google. Then nothing. They never came back. The button itself wasn't broken. So where did they go? My site is TrustCheck, and a lot of our visitors arrive from links shared on X, Instagram and Facebook. When you tap a link inside those apps, it doesn't open Chrome or Safari. It opens the app's own built-in browser. And Google refuses to sign people in inside those built-in browsers. The person taps the button, gets an error page from Google, and closes the tab. From my side, nothing failed. No error. No log line. Just a person who left. What made it worse: I had been looking at errors from those same browsers for days, and filing them as junk. My visitor insights kept recording "page errors" like: Can't find variable: CONFIG currentInset webkit.messageHandlers None of that is my code. The X, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok in-app browsers inject their own scripts into every page, and those scripts throw errors. items.title: What I Learned Choosing a Recovery Practice for Complex Delayed Data Cleanup Jobs
items.summary: Short answer: use a durable run record, bounded batches, idempotent writes, and an explicit recovery path for delayed Node.js execution. That is the best practice for a complex data cleanup job when the next weekly digest still has to run. A weekly customer digest creates a quiet operational trap: the cleanup job is delayed, then the next run arrives with twice the work and a more expensive failure. For a one-person SaaS, I choose a durable schedule with explicit leases, idempotent batches, and a recovery path before I optimize throughput. My revenue-per-hour test is simple: can I understand and restart a failed run without spending an afternoon reconstructing state? The constraint changed the design. This is a developer tool, and the job removes stale digest records for active customers after delivery. A missed run must not delete a fresh record, process the same customer twice in a harmful way, or block next week's digest. I would rather accept a few minutes of extra coordination than make recovery a manual database investigation. items.title: ECIES in TypeScript, step by step: from secp256k1 ECDH to encrypt-then-MAC
items.summary: You have someone's public key and want to send them a secret. The usual shortcut goes like this: run ECDH, use the 32 bytes of the shared secret as the AES key, encrypt in CBC with whatever IV, done. It decrypts fine in tests. But it has three problems: nobody checks that the ciphertext wasn't tampered with, the ECDH secret is used as a key as is, and if the IV or the keys repeat, the same message produces the same ciphertext. All three fit in the same OWASP Top 10 category. In this post I use it as a thread to walk, step by step and with code you can run, through how ECIES encrypts in encloom 2.0.7 (encloom/ecies): ECDH over secp256k1, SHA-512, AES-256-CBC, and HMAC-SHA256 in encrypt-then-MAC order. Not a compliance guide and not an audit. encloom isn't audited, and OWASP doesn't certify libraries. This is about what each byte does and why. The current OWASP Top 10 is the 2025 edition. Cryptographic failures are A04:2025 – Cryptographic Failures. In the 2021 edition they were A02, and the page itself says they're "Moving down two positions to #4". items.title: Splitting a tip pool in code: equal vs hours, and the penny problem
items.summary: If you build anything that pays people from a shared pool of tips, two questions come up fast: who is in the pool, and how do you divide it? The first is a business rule, so write it down before any code. A common one: only people who worked a pooled job that pay period share in the pool, not the whole roster. The second has two usual answers, and the code for both is short. Equal split. Every eligible person gets the same share. By hours. Each person's share follows the hours they worked on pooled jobs. On a $600 pool with two people, one who worked 30 hours and one who worked 10: Equal split: $300 and $300. By hours: $450 and $150. Neither is wrong. Mixing them from week to week is the problem. Divide $100 equally between three people and you get $33.333... each. Round each share to cents and you pay out $99.99, so a cent disappears. Round up and you pay $100.02. The fix is to work in whole cents, round every share down, then hand the leftover cents to the people with the largest fractional remainders. items.title: RabbitMQ 4.1 refuses clients that ask for a frame_max below 8192. amqplib before 0.10.6 does.
items.summary: I've been reading data-service release notes for the places where a server upgrade breaks a client nobody touched. RabbitMQ 4.1 has a clean example, and it mostly hits Node.js services. AMQP 0-9-1 clients and the broker agree on a maximum frame size when a connection opens. Before authentication finishes, RabbitMQ uses a smaller, fixed size. In 4.1.0 that initial size went from 4096 to 8192 bytes. The release notes give the reason: larger JWT tokens need to fit. The side effect is a new floor. A client that asks for a frame_max below 8192 can't connect to 4.1.0 or later. The broker drops the connection, and in Node the app sees ECONNRESET. The release notes name amqplib, a popular Node.js client that used a default of 4096. They say to move to 0.10.7 or later. amqplib's own changelog puts the fix one release earlier, in 0.10.6: "Use a frame_max of 131072 by default for RabbitMQ 4.1.0 compatibility." Either way, anything older asks for 4096 unless you told it otherwise. Today's server defaults, from the RabbitMQ limits page, are frame_max 131072 and initial_frame_max 8192. items.title: How I decide that a YouTube tile was actually scrolled past, without using watch history
items.summary: I got annoyed at a narrow thing on YouTube. I would scroll the home feed, skip a row of tiles on purpose, and then see the same ones come back a minute later. Watch history does not help here, because I never opened those videos. Hiding the homepage also misses the point, because I still want the feed. I just wanted the repeats to fade back. So I built a small browser extension that dims those tiles. The interesting part for me was not the overlay. It was deciding when a tile counts as seen. I need to be precise, because the name can be read the wrong way. Seen, in this project, means I already had a real look at a tile and moved on. It does not mean I watched the video. If I used YouTube's watched state, the whole idea would collapse. The tiles that bother me are the ones I refused to open. I watch tiles with IntersectionObserver and MutationObserver. The content script does not scan the page on an interval. On Home, Subscriptions, Search, and the watch sidebar, a tile is marked only if it stays in the viewport for at least two seconds and then stays out of the viewport for two seconds. items.title: YouTube's timedtext endpoint returns empty bodies from datacenter IPs — what I measured, and the panel fallback that works
items.summary: When I built a YouTube transcript export extension, the obvious data path was the timedtext endpoint: the watch page lists caption tracks, and timedtext serves them in json3, srv3, vtt and other formats. I measured it twice — once with curl, once inside a real browser — and both times it came back empty. Here is what I measured, and the fallback that actually works. On a real video page (dQw4w9WgXcQ), the watch page's captionTracks listed 6 tracks, so subtitles exist for the video. Fetching timedtext in every format returned HTTP 200 with a 0-byte body. Repeated requests then started returning 429. An empty body with a 200 status is the ambiguous case: it could be a curl artifact (missing cookies, wrong headers, no session), or the endpoint could really be refusing this client. To settle it I ran the extension's own fetch inside headless Chrome 154 on the real watch page, same-origin, with the page's own session. json3 through srv3 all came back empty (fetch-failed / empty-srv3), with no challenge page shown. items.title: Remix for Beginners: The React Framework That Uses the Web Platform Instead of Fighting It
items.summary: Remix is a full-stack React framework that takes a different approach from most of its rivals: instead of inventing new abstractions for everything, it leans on the web platform itself — real forms, real HTTP, real browser behavior. The result is a framework where pages load fast, forms work without JavaScript, and the code you write looks like the web you already know. The core idea is simple. In Remix, each route has a loader that fetches data on the server and an action that handles form submissions. Your component renders the data. There is no separate API layer to build, no client-side fetching library to configure, and no loading-spinner dance for the basic case. items.title: Why I built a live request-flow visualizer for ASP.NET Core (and what v0.4.0 adds)
items.summary: markdown Every time a request misbehaves somewhere deep inside a layered ASP.NET Core API, I hit the same wall. I know *something* went wrong between the controller and the database, but I don't know *where*, not without attaching a debugger or stitching it together from logs after the fact. That's the gap NetApiFlow is trying to close. It's an open source NuGet package that shows, live, the exact path an HTTP request takes through your own code: Controller or Endpoint, then Handler, then Services, then Repositories, then SQL. Duration per step, where a failure started, what got slow, what never ran at all. ## The constraint that shaped everything No external infrastructure. No second dashboard to deploy, no collector to babysit, no extra Docker container sitting around just for observability. The dashboard itself is an Angular app embedded straight into the NuGet package, served by your own API process. items.title: Node.js Compress and Upload AI-Generated Images to Cloud Storage: An Example Explained
items.summary: The Node.js choice to compress and upload AI-generated images to cloud storage changes once the image is part of a healthtech audit trail. A receipt image is not just an asset to display later. I need a small delivery object for normal processing and a trustworthy original for review. That makes compression useful, but it also makes public links, overwrite behavior, and browser delivery secondary concerns. Short answer: compress the generated image in Node.js with Sharp, upload the derived image under a deterministic key, and keep the original in a separate, access-controlled location. A storage API with a stable contract is a good fit when the application owns access decisions. Use a specialist object store when the storage layer itself must provide immutable retention, public delivery, or strict conditional writes. For this narrow backend step, Infrai is worth testing because its REST contract and one-key access can keep the storage adapter replaceable. I initially thought delivery simplicity would decide the whole design. It does not. The audit boundary decides it; delivery follows. Do not compress the only copy. That is the first decision. items.summary: Your app calls Supabase, and instead of data the console shows this: { "code": "PGRST116", "message": "Cannot coerce the result to a single JSON object", "details": "The result contains 0 rows", "hint": null } Older projects and older libraries print the same error as JSON object requested, multiple (or no) rows returned. The HTTP status is 406 Not Acceptable, which looks alarming and points people at headers, CORS or the wrong API key. It is none of those. It is a row-count problem, and it appears all the time in Lovable, Bolt and Vite apps that load "the current user's profile" with .single(). Below is how I read the error, the four causes I check in order, and what to change. Supabase's data API is PostgREST. By default it returns every result as an array, even when there is one item. .single() in supabase-js asks for something different: it sets the Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json header, which tells PostgREST to return one object. items.title: How to Cancel Remaining Requests When Promise.all Fails in JavaScript
items.summary: Your app has a dashboard that loads three things at the same time: the user's profile, their orders, and some recommendations. You fetch them in parallel, and you use Promise.all to wait for all three. async function getJson(path) { const response = await fetch(URL + path); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`${path} returned HTTP ${response.status}`); } return response.json(); } await Promise.all([ getJson("/profile"), getJson("/orders"), getJson("/recommendations"), ]); URL is your API's base address, such as https://api.example.com. getJson is a small wrapper around fetch that throws an error when the server answers with a failure status. Now suppose the profile request fails, so the page shows an error and stops. You'd expect the other two requests to stop too, but they keep running. Promise.all only changes when you hear about the failure. Your backend goes on executing their queries for a page that is already gone. items.title: Background Jobs 2026: Implementing Workers, Ack/Nack, Retries, and Idempotency
items.summary: Nightly payment reconciliation forces a latency-versus-cost choice: create each background job in a queue that a bounded Node.js worker pool can drain without hammering the provider. Short answer: create a durable background job queue, let a Node.js worker consume one bounded reconciliation slice at a time, ack only after an atomic idempotency record is committed, nack retryable failures with delay, and send exhausted or permanent failures to a dead letter queue. The queue library matters less than those state transitions. I would benchmark end-to-end completion time, provider calls per settled account, and retry volume before tuning concurrency. Otherwise, “faster” is just a guess with a larger bill attached. The unit of work should be a stable slice, not “reconcile everything.” In this example, one job represents one merchant account for one settlement date. Its identity is merchantId + settlementDate; its payload contains no credentials and no mutable retry counter supplied by a caller. items.title: AWS Lambda Web Functions vs Classic Lambda vs EC2/ECS
items.summary: Lambda was never the wrong place for APIs. One request per box was. If you are building a Node.js API, Lambda usually is not on the list. You reach for a container on ECS, or an instance on EC2. On 12 October 2026 AWS launched Lambda Web Functions, and the reasons behind that instinct need a second look. The instinct was never superstition. Classic Lambda, which AWS now calls Event Functions, had three properties that fought against a normal web server. It wanted a handler, not a server. Your code was a function, handler(event, context), that Lambda called once per request. An Express app expects to own a port and a request loop, so it needed an adapter library to translate Lambda events into HTTP requests and back. One request per environment. An execution environment is the small, isolated virtual machine that runs your code. In classic Lambda, each environment handles exactly one request at a time. A hundred requests at the same moment means a hundred environments. Wall-clock billing. items.title: 5 Ways Node.js Teams Build Incremental Indexing for SaaS Help Centers
items.summary: Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For an edtech help center serving several tenants, incremental indexing should update only changed chunks, while every answer still carries the tenant and document version that produced it. The useful boundary is simple: ingestion turns a published article into retrieval units; querying selects candidates under tenant and freshness filters; the answer layer cites those candidates. Keep those stages observable and independently testable. A reranker can improve ordering, but it cannot repair a document that was never indexed or a filter that leaked another tenant. Start with a retrieval contract, not a vendor endpoint. Define the unit (a heading plus a few paragraphs, for example), the metadata (tenant_id, article_id, locale, version, updated_at), and the freshness promise. An incremental worker can hash normalized content and skip unchanged units. A delete event should remove the old version, not merely append a newer one. I once assumed a timestamp was enough to detect changes. It wasn't: a CMS import rounded timestamps to seconds, so two edits could share a value.

items.title: Invoice PDFs in a Multi-Tenant Backend: Who Can Download What, and Where the Edges Are
items.summary: An invoice PDF looks trivial until you add tenants, customers, and drafts. Then every download is an access-control decision. Here is how we handle it in StoreFlux, and where the edges are. There are two download routes. Staff use the admin route, and customers use the storefront route for their own orders. Both run the same query handler. The handler resolves the invoice first. For an order, it looks up the invoice that belongs to that order and the current tenant. If no invoice exists, the answer is not found, because there is nothing to render. Then it checks ownership. A super admin can read across tenants. Everyone else must match the invoice's tenant, or the request throws an unauthorized tenant error. A customer gets one more rule. They can only open invoices where the invoice's user is them, and a draft is never shown to a customer. For anyone else, the handler returns nothing, which becomes a not-found response. We chose not-found over forbidden on purpose, because a forbidden answer would confirm that the invoice exists. items.title: Rate-Limited Webhook Queue Consumer: Node.js Republish for Reservation Expiry
items.summary: The page says a rate-limited webhook queue stopped sending reservation-expiry events on time. The consumer is alive and its dashboard is green, but neither fact tells the on-call engineer which partner refused a webhook, how old the affected event is, or when it can run again. TL;DR: make the Node.js consumer own the delivery policy, even if a queue owns delivery. Acknowledge only a confirmed webhook success. On 429, parse Retry-After, lower concurrency for that destination, and republish a successor with a delay and incremented attempt metadata. Use bounded backoff for temporary failures, preserve the event ID, and make reservation expiry idempotent because standard queues can deliver more than once. Page on oldest eligible event age and backlog growth by destination, not on worker liveness. This division also makes a later queue migration less dangerous: the adapter handles publish, consume, acknowledge, and statistics, while application code retains the rules that decide whether a reservation expiry is done, deferred, or terminal. items.summary: Seller leads are the ones real estate agents actually pay for. A buyer lead fills out a form and disappears into a dozen other agents' inboxes. A seller who wants to know what their house is worth is a few months away from signing a listing agreement. That is why the "What's my home worth?" widget exists on almost every agent site, and why most of them are either a third party iframe or a single form that asks for an email before it gives anything back. The Home valuation funnel in Facade is my attempt at a version that respects the visitor and still captures the lead. Here is how I built it. Order matters more than design in a lead funnel. The first field sets the tone, and "Email address" as the first field says "we want your data." "Property address" says "tell us about the house." Same form, different first question, very different completion. There is a practical reason too. The address is the one piece of information the visitor has that an agent cannot get elsewhere, and it is the field that feels least like a commitment. items.title: How I keep bots out of my own analytics, with no cookies and no third-party scripts
items.summary: I run a small file converter, imageconvert.art. Like most side projects, I wanted to know one thing: are real people using it? I didn't want Google Analytics (cookie banner, a third-party script on every page, data I don't need). So I wrote a tiny page-view counter of my own. On the first day it said I had visitors. Lots of them. Most of them, it turned out, weren't people. Here's how I fixed it with five small checks. No cookies, no fingerprinting, nothing stored that identifies anyone. Count a view every time the server renders a page. That counts everything: Googlebot, Bingbot, uptime monitors, SEO crawlers, link previews from chat apps, and the random scanners that hit every new domain looking for /wp-login.php. items.title: Your iOS App Says “Offline”—But Is It? Debugging API Failures With a VPN Enabled
items.summary: A user connects their iPhone to a VPN, opens your app and sees: No internet connection. Please try again. They switch to another app, which works. Your app may have encountered a real failure. But “no internet” might be the wrong diagnosis. A hostname lookup can fail. A secure connection can fail. An API can return an authentication error. The response can arrive successfully and then fail JSON decoding. A failed API operation does not automatically mean the device is offline—or that the VPN caused the failure. The first useful fix is to preserve those distinctions in your networking code. Think of an API operation as several stages: Establish a usable network connection. Resolve the destination hostname when needed. Establish the secure connection. Exchange the HTTP request and response. Interpret the response body. This is a debugging model, not a claim that every request creates a new connection or performs a fresh DNS lookup. Connections and lookup results can be reused. The point is that failures at different stages need different handling. items.title: Obfuscating source-generated code safely
items.summary: A source generator is a compiler plugin that reads your code and emits more code into the same compilation. By the time the C# compiler finishes, the generated files are just part of your assembly — same metadata tables, same IL, no marker in the output that distinguishes a method you wrote from one the generator wrote. Which raises the obvious question for an obfuscator: when Nebula renames your types and members, what happens to code that was generated around them? The answer is better than you'd expect, with one twist. Generators resolve names at compile time, which is exactly the property that makes code rename-safe. But the way they do it is by writing your names down as string literals, and those literals survive renaming verbatim — occasionally telling an attacker what a method used to be called. The whole reason obfuscation breaks things is runtime name lookup. items.title: Licensing an MSIX-packaged Windows app
items.summary: Ask a .NET desktop developer where their app keeps its settings and they will say %LocalAppData%. Ask what happens to those files when the app is uninstalled and they will say "nothing, that is the user's data". Both answers are right for an MSI. Both are wrong for an MSIX package — and MSIX is now how desktop apps arrive on Windows machines, whether through winget install, an Intune deployment, or the Store. That matters to licensing more than to almost anything else an app writes, because a licensing SDK keeps exactly the kind of small, important files whose location and lifetime you need to understand: a signed activation lease that lets the app run offline, a local timestamp that stops a trial from being restarted, a record of the last time the clock was seen. This post looks at what the Keyright SDK writes, where those bytes actually land inside a packaged app, what an uninstall does to them, and how to make the whole thing explicit instead of letting a file-system filter decide. A Keyright client is initialised once with the product name and the embedded public key, and from then on it keeps up to three files for that product: {LocalApplicationData}\Keyright\{product}\lease.j

items.title: Licensing a .NET app on Linux and macOS
items.summary: The Keyright SDK does not care which operating system it is on. Keyright.NET targets netstandard2.0 and net8.0, Validate() is pure computation over bytes, and ActivateAsync is an HTTPS call. Deploy a licensed worker on Ubuntu or ship a Mac build of your desktop app and the same code runs. That is the good news, and it is also why the three platform differences that do matter tend to surface as a support ticket rather than a compile error. A licensing SDK depends on three things the platform provides: somewhere per-user to keep a small signed file, a stable identity for the machine, and — less obviously — an application that gets relaunched often enough to refresh what it cached. On Windows those are %LocalAppData%, the registry MachineGuid, and the fact that desktop apps start every morning. Off Windows all three are different, and a Keyright integration that was tested on a developer's Windows laptop can quietly do the wrong thing on the Linux box it is deployed to. This post is the Linux and macOS version of the story: where the files go, what the fingerprint is made of, how to give a systemd service a home, and the refresh loop a process that never restarts needs. items.title: What marks an extension method when decompiled
items.summary: An extension method is one of the purest examples of C# sugar that evaporates in IL. You write this on the first parameter, call it as text.WordCount(), and feel like you added a method to string. The runtime sees none of that. There is a static method, there is a static call, and there is one attribute — [Extension] — left behind like a note that says this could have been written with a dot. A decompiler's whole job here is to read that note and decide to print the dot, then get the precedence right so a ten-operator LINQ pipeline comes back as a pipeline and not a ten-deep nest. This post walks it for Glass.NET. Start with the definition. A trivial extension on string: public static class StringExtensions { public static int WordCount(this string s) => s.Split((char[]?)null, StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries).Length; } Compile it and look at what this became. It is gone from the parameter — s is an ordinary string parameter — and in its place are two [Extension] attributes, one on the method and one on the class: .class public abstract sealed auto ansi beforefieldinit StringExtensions extends [System.Runtime]System.Object { .custom instance void [System.Runtime]System.Runtime

items.summary: The blog XDA Developers reports that a Claude enthusiast used the AI assistant to make a language model that runs off a floppy disk. "And you can stick it on a DOS computer to boot." The language models "runs at a respectable speed, given that it's running off a CPU that was designed decades before LLMs were even a thing." Over on the ClaudeAI subreddit, user wollymonjak showed off this really impressive feat... [I]t's not going to be a particularly powerful AI; in fact, wollymonjak notes that if you ask something too complex or too long, it starts spitting out nonsense. But who cares about that when you're using a language model on DOS? The same blog also notes that "the iPhone Duo hasn't been out for too long, and someone has already gotten Windows 11 on it." As spotted by TechSpot, this cool feat was performed by Ammaar Reshi over on X. Their project is called WindowsiOS, and its goal is to get Windows 11 running on an iPhone Duo without jailbreaking. Usually, when we cover a project coded up by AI, Claude is the one that called the shots; this time, Reshi opted to use Gemini 4 Carbon, Google's flagship model. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.summary: I've spent 7+ years in product design, most of it on design systems for other people's products. This year I built one for myself: GYM Paper, a free workout and nutrition tracker for iPhone and Apple Watch. It passed App Review, it's on the App Store, and today the whole project is open source under MIT. Your data stays on your device and in your own iCloud. Design system first. Colors, type and spacing are Figma variables, mirrored one-to-one as SwiftUI tokens. Once that layer existed, most new screens became assembly of existing parts. AI for the first draft, me for the decisions. Claude wrote most of the first-draft code. Every product decision, and every "no", was still mine. Tested at the gym. Every build went through real sets. It has a "Show in menu bar" toggle, and opening the app again from Finder should bring a hidden icon back. Then I tried the case I'd skipped: launch with the icon already hidden, then reopen. The handler ran (I logged it), the value became true, and it was false again within 100 ms. I added a KVO observer on the key and logged Thread.callStackSymbols on every change. items.title: Noticing "Shift held during a file drag" from a macOS menu bar app
items.summary: Convrt is a small open-source menu bar app: you start dragging files from Finder or the desktop, hold Shift, and a wheel opens under the cursor. Drop on a slice and the file is converted (HEIC to JPG, MOV to MP4, images to PDF and so on). The interesting part isn't the conversion. It's how a background app with no window finds out that some other app is dragging files and that Shift is down, without breaking the drag. Here is how it works in the shipped code. A menu bar app never gets these events directly, so it uses a global monitor: let mask: NSEvent.EventTypeMask = [.leftMouseDown, .leftMouseDragged, .leftMouseUp, .flagsChanged, .scrollWheel, .keyDown] monitor = NSEvent.addGlobalMonitorForEvents(matching: mask) { [weak self] event in self?.handle(event) } Global monitors only work with the Accessibility permission (and Input Monitoring for keys), and they only observe: you can't consume or change the events. That's fine here, because the drag should carry on untouched. A global leftMouseDragged event says nothing about what is being dragged. items.title: Supabase email sign-in and a profiles table for iOS, done safely
items.summary: Almost every iOS app I start needs the same first hour of work: email sign-in, a place to keep per-user data, and a way to make sure users can only touch their own rows. Supabase gives you most of it. The part people get wrong is the profiles table, because the obvious version is also the insecure one. This post walks through the setup I use: the SQL, the Swift, and the three mistakes to avoid. It assumes you know basic SwiftUI and have a free Supabase project. Supabase Auth stores credentials in auth.users. You don't add your own columns there. Instead you create a public.profiles table whose primary key is the auth user's id: create table if not exists public.profiles ( id uuid primary key references auth.users (id) on delete cascade, email text, full_name text, avatar_url text, created_at timestamptz not null default now(), updated_at timestamptz not null default now() ); on delete cascade matters: when the auth user is deleted, the profile goes with it. No orphans. The key in your app is public. Anyone can extract it. So the key is not your security. Row Level Security (RLS) is. alter table public.profiles enable row level security; -- signed-out clients get nothing revoke all

items.title: How to Tell If Your Mac App Has Been Cracked
items.summary: Search your app name plus "crack", "cracked" or "free download" on Google, warez and torrent sites, and GitHub. Record those listings by URL and screenshot; do not download from them. If you already have a copy, inspect it with codesign -dv --verbose=4 and spctl -a -vv without launching it, then compare Team ID and cdhash to your release. https://fortifie.xyz/cracked runs the listings search faster, a search of public listings, not proof. This guide is for the developer who published the app, not for someone seeing a Gatekeeper warning. A cracked copy can appear on a warez site, a torrent index or GitHub without showing up in your analytics. Start with a search, not a download. On Google, query your app name plus "crack", "cracked", "free download" or "dmg", and quote the name if it is generic. Repeat those queries on Mac warez sites and torrent indexes, then search GitHub for the app name, your bundle ID, or a distinctive Info.plist string. Do not download anything from a crack, warez or torrent listing; record that listing by URL and screenshot only. items.summary: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). items.title: Building a read-aloud screen: phrases, tappable words and a finger that drifts
items.summary: Background A lot of what I read is still on paper: letters from the bank, school handouts, a recipe, a library book. I often want to listen to them instead, and I want to follow the words while I listen, so my eyes have something to hold on to. So I built Outloud Reader. You take a photo of a printed page (or open a PDF, or paste text), the app reads it out loud, and the phrase being spoken is highlighted on screen. It runs on iOS and Android, and it can translate a page before reading it. This post is about the reading screen, the part people look at for minutes at a time. It turned out to be the hardest screen in the app to get right. What I wanted from it: the current phrase highlighted, the current sentence easy to find, the rest of the page calm; tap any word to jump the audio there; a "just listen" mode with the text hidden, which you can still peek at; Japanese, Chinese and Thai behaving like any other language. Word-by-word highlighting, like karaoke. It is still in the code as an option, but it was exhausting to watch. items.title: I built a free Mac dictation app that never sends your voice to a server
items.summary: A few months ago my wrists started aching by mid-afternoon. I type for a living, most days for nine to twelve hours, and by evening I was closing the laptop instead of answering one more email. I tried the voice to text apps people recommend. A couple of them are good. Every one I tried wanted a monthly subscription and sent my voice to a server before the text came back, and I've written enough software to know that audio can sit on somebody else's disk for as long as they like. So I built my own, over a few weekends that turned into a few months. I wanted to see whether small open models could do the whole job on a laptop people already own. The result is Purr, a free, open-source menu bar app for macOS. You hold Right Option, talk and let go, and the words get typed into whatever text field has focus. It doesn't need an account, and nothing it hears leaves your Mac. Once the models have downloaded, it works offline. What it does Dictation is the main thing. If you'd rather see words appear while you talk, Smart Typing types as you speak instead of waiting for the key to come up. Voice Edit works on text you've already written. items.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic (15 minute read)

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

items.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)

It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.
